Reflection across the core circle sends a representative $(x, y)$ to $(1 - x, y)$. This descends to a map $\tau\colon M \to M$, $\tau([x, y]) = [1 - x, y]$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Compatibility]
Reflection respects the gluing, so $\tau$ is well defined.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $(0, y) \sim (1, -y)$, then reflecting both gives $(1, y)$ and $(0, -y)$; and $(1, y) \sim (0, -y)$ holds by the second boundary case (since $y = -(-y)$). Hence $\tau$ maps equivalent points to equivalent points.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The twist is negation]
For every $z \in M$, $\ \val(\tau(z)) = -\,\val(z)$. Moreover $\tau$ is an involution ($\tau \circ \tau = \mathrm{id}$), and its fixed points are exactly the classes with $x = \tfrac12$, i.e. the central circle.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
On representatives,
\[
\varphi(1 - x, y) = y\big(2(1-x) - 1\big) = y(1 - 2x) = -\,y(2x - 1) = -\varphi(x, y).
\]
Applying reflection twice returns $x$, so $\tau^2 = \mathrm{id}$. A point is fixed by $\tau$ iff $[1-x, y] = [x, y]$; away from the boundary this forces $1 - x = x$, i.e. $x = \tfrac12$, which is the central circle (where the value is $0$).
\end{proof}

Theorem is the rigorous meaning of ``going around the band flips the sign.'' The pair $\{\mathrm{id}, \tau\}$ is a $\Z/2$ action, and $\val$ is anti-invariant under it: the surface carries a genuine $\Z/2$-grading in which $\tau$ implements multiplication by $-1$ on values.

\subsection{The zero fibre}

\begin{theorem}[Zero set]
For all $x, y$, $\ \val([x, y]) = 0 \iff y = 0 \ \text{or}\ x = \tfrac12$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\varphi(x,y) = y(2x-1) = 0$ iff one factor vanishes: $y = 0$ or $2x - 1 = 0$, i.e. $x = \tfrac12$. Conversely each condition makes a factor zero.
\end{proof}

Geometrically the zero fibre is the union of the \emph{zero section} $\{y = 0\}$ and the \emph{central circle} $\{x = \tfrac12\}$ --- two transverse curves. Note that $\tau$ fixes the central circle pointwise and preserves the zero section, consistent with $\val \circ \tau = -\val$.

\section{The collapse of the M\"obius integers}

We now test the arithmetic proposal directly.

\begin{definition}[Integer embedding]
For $n \in \Z$, $n \neq 0$, define
\[
e(n) = \Big[\ \tfrac12 + \tfrac{1}{2n},\ \ |n|\ \Big] \in M.
\]
As $|n| \to \infty$ the width coordinate tends to $\tfrac12$ (the core circle) and the height records the magnitude --- the ``spiral'' of the conjecture.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Embedding evaluates to the sign]
For every nonzero integer $n$,
\[
\val(e(n)) = \sgn(n) = \begin{cases} +1, & n > 0,\\ -1, & n < 0.\end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Directly,
\[
\val(e(n)) = |n|\left(2\Big(\tfrac12 + \tfrac{1}{2n}\Big) - 1\right) = |n|\left(1 + \tfrac1n - 1\right) = \frac{|n|}{n}.
\]
If $n > 0$ then $|n| = n$ and the quotient is $+1$; if $n < 0$ then $|n| = -n$ and the quotient is $-1$. In both cases $\val(e(n)) = \sgn(n)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Collapse and non-injectivity]
The values coincide across all positive integers and across all negative integers; e.g. $\val(e(1)) = \val(e(2)) = +1$ while $1 \neq 2$. Hence the map $n \mapsto \val(e(n))$ is not injective, and the image of $\Z\setminus\{0\}$ is exactly the two-element set $\{-1, +1\}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Immediate from the previous theorem: the value depends on $n$ only through its sign. Two integers with the same sign have equal value, so injectivity fails, and the image is $\{-1,+1\}$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Consequences for the conjectured ring}

The collapse dismantles the arithmetic program at its foundation, before any ring axiom is in play.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{No faithful copy of $\Z$.} A number system requires distinct numbers to be distinct. Here all positive integers share the value $+1$ and all negative integers share $-1$. The embedding is drastically non-injective.
\item \textbf{No one-point compactification of $\Z$.} The proposed identification of $+1$ and $-1$ ``at the twist'' is contradicted: the values $+1$ and $-1$ are in fact \emph{distinct}, while the \emph{magnitudes} a compactification would need have all been erased.
\item \textbf{No prime factorization, no twist prime.} Factorization presupposes distinguishable elements $2, 3, 6, \dots$ with a multiplicative law. But $2_+$, $3_+$, and $6_+$ all evaluate to $+1$: there is no multiplicative structure to support $6 = 2_+ \cdot 3_+$, nor a ``twist prime'' $-1$.
\item \textbf{The integral-domain question is vacuous.} The conjectured witness of zero-divisors cannot be posed, because there is no well-defined multiplication compatible with $\val$ that would make the claimed factors nonzero and their product zero.
\end{enumerate}

The failure is \emph{structural}: $\val$ is a scalar invariant that on the embedded integers depends only on sign, because the width coordinate $\tfrac12 + \tfrac1{2n}$ produces exactly the cancellation $1 + \tfrac1n - 1$.

\section{What survives: the $\Z/2$ content of the twist}

The negative verdict sharpens the geometric intuition. The twist $\tau$ is an involution with $\val \circ \tau = -\val$; thus $\{\mathrm{id}, \tau\} \cong \Z/2$ acts on $M$, with $\val$ an odd function. The fixed locus of $\tau$ is the central circle $x = \tfrac12$, contained in the zero fibre. The correct interpretation of the ``twist prime $-1$'' is therefore \emph{the generator of $\Z/2$}, not a prime in a ring: orientation contributes a \emph{grading}, a single bit, not an arithmetic atom.

This matches the standard picture of $M \to S^1$ as the tautological nonorientable real line bundle: it admits no nowhere-zero global section, and the monodromy around the base is multiplication by $-1$ on the fibre. The value map $\varphi$ is a section-like scalar invariant, anti-invariant under the deck action --- precisely a $\Z/2$-graded object, not a ring of numbers.

\end{itemize}

\section{Applications and interpretation}

The chief application is methodological. The analysis is a compact case study in how a geometrically motivated algebraic conjecture can fail: not through a subtle inconsistency in the axioms, but because the very map connecting geometry to number destroys the magnitude information arithmetic needs. The surviving structure --- orientation reversal as an order-two symmetry acting by negation --- is the kind of $\Z/2$-grading that pervades mathematics and physics: real line bundles and their obstruction, $\Z/2$-graded (super) vector spaces, and, loosely, the sign a wavefunction can acquire. The slogan ``orientation is like spin'' is best cashed out as ``orientation is a $\Z/2$-grading,'' not ``orientation is a prime.''

\section{Discussion}

The proposal conflated two roles the twist might play. As a \emph{symmetry} it behaves impeccably and delivers exactly the negation intuition promised. As an \emph{arithmetic generator} it has nothing to work with, because the chosen embedding retains only sign. Nonorientability naturally produces $\Z/2$ data; inflating this single bit into a full arithmetic overreaches. The transversality in the zero fibre --- the zero section meeting the central circle, which is exactly the fixed set of the twist --- is the geometric signature of the sign becoming undefined.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{itemize}

\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

Modeling the M\"obius band as $(\R\times\R)/\!\sim$ with value map $\varphi(x, y) = y(2x - 1)$, we established that the value map descends and is surjective, that the twist is an involution acting as exact negation with the central circle as fixed set, and that the zero fibre is the union of the zero section and the central circle.
